title: The Invisible Translator

lines.text: Good afternoon. I'd like to begin with a small confession: most of you have read a translator this week without noticing. That, I'm afraid, is rather the point of the profession, and also its central problem.
For a long time, the highest compliment a translation could receive was that it read as if it had never been translated. Fluency was treated as a virtue and visibility as a failing.
I'd like to question that. Not because fluent translations are bad, but because the ideal quietly hides a great many decisions.

Consider a single sentence of dialogue in which one character addresses another with an intimate pronoun in the original. English has no such distinction. So the translator must choose: add a warm adverb, change the verb, or simply lose the intimacy.

Whichever she picks, the reader will never know a choice was made. We tend to say the translator renders the text, as though the text were a block of stone she merely carries from one room to another.
A translator's day is mostly spent on tiny dilemmas that nobody will ever thank her for solving.
The text is not a block of stone. It's closer to rebuilding a house from the photographs, with different bricks and a different climate.

Now, some publishers have begun to print the translator's name on the cover. Welcome as that is, I'd urge a little caution. A name on the cover is not the same as a fair fee. I can tell you that the two do not always travel together.

There is also a counter-argument, and it deserves a hearing. If translators draw attention to themselves, the author may be upstaged. A reader picks up a novel to meet the author, not her interpreter.
I find that argument half persuasive. The reader does meet the author, but only through a particular pair of hands.
That sounds abstract, so let me be concrete.
Years ago I translated a novel whose narrator was notoriously evasive. In the original, the evasion came from verb tenses that slid about without warning.
English tenses are much less obliging. I could have smoothed it out, and my editor, bless her, begged me to. The result would have been perfectly readable and entirely wrong.
So I kept the slippage and added a short note explaining why. Several reviewers called the note intrusive. I called it honesty, though I concede that honesty and vanity are not mutually exclusive.
What I'm suggesting is a more modest ideal than invisibility. Call it candour: a translation that does its job well and doesn't pretend that it had no choices to make.
For next week, please compare two published translations of the same opening paragraph and list every decision you can detect. You will find more than you expect.

questions.q: What is the lecturer's attitude to the idea that a translation should read as if it had never been translated?
options: She dismisses all fluent translations as poor
She accepts it as the profession's proper aim
She considers it outdated but largely harmless
She regards it as an ideal that conceals choices
questions.explain_es: Actitud. Cuestiona el ideal sin condenar la fluidez: 'I'd like to question that' y 'the ideal quietly hides a great many decisions'.

questions.q: What does she imply when she says that a name on the cover is not the same as a fair fee?
options: Translators ought to decline being named
Public credit does not ensure fair payment
Publishers rarely print translators' names
Payment rises whenever names are printed
questions.explain_es: Implicatura. Insinúa que el reconocimiento y el pago justo van por separado: 'the two do not always travel together'.

questions.q: The lecturer kept the shifting tenses of the original narrator in her translation.
questions.explain_es: Detalle. Lo dice así: 'So I kept the slippage and added a short note explaining why.'

questions.q: Why does she describe translating the evasive narrator?
options: To illustrate how smoothing could betray the original
To show that English tenses are poorly designed
To prove that editors always disagree with translators
To complain about the reviewers who criticised her
questions.explain_es: Propósito. Ilustra el riesgo de alisar el original: 'The result would have been perfectly readable and entirely wrong.'

questions.q: What does she suggest by saying that honesty and vanity are not mutually exclusive?
options: She thinks honesty and vanity are the same thing
She believes the reviewers were entirely right
She suspects her note may also have been self-regarding
She regrets adding the note to the book
questions.explain_es: Ironía. Se burla de sí misma: 'honesty and vanity are not mutually exclusive' admite un posible toque de vanidad en su nota.

questions.q: She argues that readers never meet the author when they read a translation.
questions.explain_es: Detalle. Dice lo contrario: 'The reader does meet the author, but only through a particular pair of hands.'

dictation: The result would have been perfectly readable and entirely wrong.
A name on the cover is not the same as a fair fee.

title: Should Universities Abolish Grades?
focus: Concession, hedging and rebuttal in academic argument

lines.text: Welcome to the Humanities Forum. Tonight's motion: this house would abolish numerical grades in universities. Professor Adler will propose, Doctor Okoye will oppose. Professor, the floor is yours.
Thank you. Let me begin by conceding what the other side will say: grades are efficient. Employers like them, administrators adore them, and students can compare themselves at a glance.
My complaint is that a number gives the appearance of precision where none exists. Two examiners can read the same essay and differ by a whole classification, and nobody loses sleep over it.
Worse, students learn to chase the mark rather than the idea. I have lost count of the number of times I have been asked, with perfect sincerity, whether something will be on the test.
I'm grateful for the candour, Professor, because I think you've just made my argument for me. Students ask that question because they are rational, not because they are shallow.
Remove grades and the pressure doesn't vanish. It simply goes underground, into references, reputations and the quiet prejudices of whoever happens to be writing the report.
That's a fair worry, but it assumes the present system is neutral, which it plainly isn't.
I wouldn't claim it is neutral. I claim that a number can be challenged, appealed and audited, whereas a warm paragraph of narrative feedback cannot be.
Professor Adler, a quick response?
Narrative feedback can be audited perfectly well if one is willing to spend the money. Which, I suspect, is where this debate really lives.
On that, at least, we agree. The cost of careful assessment is borne by lecturers' evenings and weekends, and no motion tonight will change that.
Then perhaps the motion is slightly too bold. I would settle for a system in which the grade is the last thing a student sees, not the first.
Now that I could support. Feedback first, mark afterwards, and a mark that is never the only thing on the page.
Forgive me, but that sounds suspiciously as though the two of you are about to agree, and the audience has paid good money to see a fight.
Do forgive us. We'll try to disagree about something else over the sandwiches.
Please do. We'll now take questions from the floor.

questions.q: What is Professor Adler's attitude to numerical grades at the start of the debate?
options: He mocks their critics but defends their precision
He denies their convenience but trusts their accuracy
He praises their fairness but dislikes their cost
He admits their convenience but doubts their precision
questions.explain_es: Actitud. Concede su utilidad pero duda de su exactitud: 'grades are efficient' y 'a number gives the appearance of precision where none exists'.

questions.q: What does Doctor Okoye imply when she says that Adler has just made her argument for her?
options: Students react rationally to how they are assessed
Examiners are more consistent than he suggests
Students are too shallow to understand ideas
Professor Adler has privately abandoned the motion
questions.explain_es: Implicatura. Si los alumnos preguntan por el examen es por lógica del sistema: 'Students ask that question because they are rational, not because they are shallow.'

questions.q: Professor Adler claims that the present grading system is completely neutral.
questions.explain_es: Detalle. Afirma lo contrario: 'it assumes the present system is neutral, which it plainly isn't'.

questions.q: Why does Doctor Okoye mention 'a warm paragraph of narrative feedback'?
options: To suggest that it is always more accurate
To argue that students dislike receiving it
To show that it is harder to appeal against
To prove that it costs lecturers nothing
questions.explain_es: Propósito. Contrapone la nota, que se puede impugnar, al comentario narrativo: 'a number can be challenged, appealed and audited, whereas a warm paragraph ... cannot be'.

questions.q: What is the tone of the chair's remark that the audience has paid good money to see a fight?
options: Formal warning about the debate rules
Sincere worry about ticket refunds
Genuine anger at the speakers' behaviour
Teasing complaint about a lack of conflict
questions.explain_es: Ironía. Bromea con que los dos oradores están a punto de coincidir: 'sounds suspiciously as though the two of you are about to agree'.

questions.q: By the end, both speakers support giving feedback before the mark.
questions.explain_es: Detalle. Adler: 'the grade is the last thing a student sees'; Okoye: 'Feedback first, mark afterwards'.

dictation: Feedback first, mark afterwards, and a mark that is never the only thing on the page.
My complaint is that a number gives the appearance of precision where none exists.

title: Eighty Words
focus: Understatement, wry humour and diplomatic phrasing

lines.text: On Arts Tonight we're in the museum world, and specifically in the small rectangle of text that sits beside every object. The wall label. Doctor Amara Osei has spent twenty years writing them. Amara, is it an art?
It's a craft, which is a less glamorous word and, I'd say, a more honest one. Eighty words, perhaps, to explain an object that took someone a year to make.
Eighty words isn't much.
It's a sonnet's worth of discipline with none of the applause. People imagine we write what we know. In fact the job is mostly deciding what to leave out.
And who decides?
Ideally a committee of curators, an educator and, increasingly, someone from the community the object came from. Ideally. In practice it's often three people and a deadline.
I've read labels that seem to have been written by someone who would rather you weren't looking at the object at all.
Ha. Yes, there's a certain kind of label that says, in effect, 'This is important, and you wouldn't understand why.' I wrote a few of those in my youth, I'm sorry to say.
What's the worst offence?
Jargon, without question. A label that tells you a vase is 'a vessel typifying liminal domestic practice' has failed. It has taken a beautiful thing and put a fence around it.
Some visitors, though, actually like a bit of difficulty.
Some do, and I wouldn't want to patronise them. But a label isn't a place for showing off. If you want to be clever, write a book. If you want to be useful, write a label.
What about objects with difficult histories? Things taken during colonial rule, for example.

Those are the labels I lose sleep over. It's no longer acceptable to write 'acquired in the nineteenth century' and leave the reader to guess how. Vagueness there isn't neutral; it's a way of looking away.
Does honesty cost you anything?
Occasionally a trustee frowns. But visitors, in my experience, can cope with a lot more truth than institutions give them credit for.
Amara Osei, thank you for your time and, I should say, for your restraint. You were allowed all of eighty words.
And I've used rather more. Don't tell my editor.

questions.q: Why does Doctor Osei prefer the word 'craft' to 'art'?
options: She resents the lack of public recognition
She prefers the humbler word as more honest
She thinks the word 'art' is too vague
She believes labels deserve artistic prizes
questions.explain_es: Actitud. Elige la palabra más modesta por ser más veraz: 'a less glamorous word and, I'd say, a more honest one'.

questions.q: What does she imply about labels that say 'This is important, and you wouldn't understand why'?
options: Such labels are aimed at specialists
Such labels are written by novices only
Such labels explain objects too fully
Such labels talk down to visitors
questions.explain_es: Implicatura. Esas etiquetas tratan al visitante con condescendencia; ella añade enseguida 'I wouldn't want to patronise them'.

questions.q: Doctor Osei says that vague wording about how an object was acquired is not neutral.
questions.explain_es: Detalle. Lo dice así: 'Vagueness there isn't neutral; it's a way of looking away.'

questions.q: Why does she say 'If you want to be clever, write a book'?
options: To criticise visitors who enjoy difficulty
To suggest that curators ought to write more books
To explain why labels are so short
To insist that labels should serve the visitor
questions.explain_es: Propósito. Defiende que la etiqueta debe servir al visitante, no lucir al autor: 'If you want to be useful, write a label.'

questions.q: How should the host's remark about her 'restraint' be understood?
options: He sincerely praises her brevity
He apologises for interrupting her
He teases her for having talked at length
He criticises the museum's word limits
questions.explain_es: Ironía. Bromea porque ella se ha extendido bastante más de ochenta palabras, y ella lo admite: 'I've used rather more'.

questions.q: Doctor Osei says that visitors cannot cope with much truth about difficult histories.
questions.explain_es: Detalle. Dice lo contrario: 'visitors ... can cope with a lot more truth than institutions give them credit for'.

dictation: Vagueness there isn't neutral; it's a way of looking away.
If you want to be useful, write a label.

title: The Library That Refuses to Die

lines.text: Good evening. Our subject tonight is the public library, an institution that is routinely declared dead and stubbornly refuses to lie down. With me are Tobias Wren, a library director, and Ife Adeyemi, who builds search tools for a living. Tobias, a provocative opening: why does anyone need a library when they have a phone?
A fair question, and one I'm asked weekly. My short answer is that a phone gives you answers, whereas a library gives you a place to be without having to buy anything.
I'd quarrel with 'answers', if I may. What a phone gives you is a great many plausible-sounding answers, and nobody tells you which to trust.
Quite. A librarian's real skill isn't knowing facts. It's knowing which source is likely to be worth the reader's time.
Which, I'll admit, is a skill my own industry has been remarkably slow to copy.
Ife, that's a striking confession for a technologist.
I try to confess one thing a year, and then get back to work.
Tobias, there's a stereotype of libraries as quiet places for the elderly. Is that fair?

It's half true, and the true half is nothing to be ashamed of. Our busiest hours are after school, and the people who need us most are often those without a quiet room or a reliable connection at home.
That, I think, is the point people miss. We talk about access to information as if it were purely about content. It's about the conditions in which you can use it.
Exactly. A table, a lamp and no one asking why you're there.
Is there a danger of nostalgia here? Libraries are lovely, but love isn't a funding model.

That's the sharpest question of the evening, and I'll try to match it. We can't live on affection. Councils fund what they can measure, so we've had to learn to measure things like job applications completed and children who borrowed their first book.
I'd add a cautionary note. The moment you measure something, you start managing for the number. If library success becomes a footfall figure, you'll get gimmicks.
A point I accept, though I'd rather have gimmicks than closure.
Fair. I withdraw the objection, and substitute a mild eyebrow.
On that note of eyebrows, we'll take our first caller.

questions.q: What is Tobias's attitude to the stereotype of libraries as quiet places for the elderly?
options: He rejects it as entirely unfounded
He accepts part of it without embarrassment
He is ashamed that it still applies
He finds it amusing but harmless
questions.explain_es: Actitud. Admite parte de verdad sin sentir vergüenza: 'It's half true, and the true half is nothing to be ashamed of.'

questions.q: What does Ife imply by calling the ranking of reliable sources 'a skill my own industry has been remarkably slow to copy'?
options: Her industry has refused to hire librarians
Technology firms have neglected source reliability
Librarians' skills are impossible to automate
Search tools have always ranked sources well
questions.explain_es: Implicatura. Reconoce con ironía que las empresas tecnológicas no han imitado la habilidad de juzgar fuentes: 'knowing which source is likely to be worth the reader's time'.

questions.q: Tobias says that libraries are busiest in the early morning.
questions.explain_es: Detalle. Dice: 'Our busiest hours are after school'.

questions.q: Why does Ife warn that the library will 'get gimmicks'?
options: To claim that visitors dislike new activities
To warn that targets can distort what libraries do
To insist that libraries should ignore funding
To argue that footfall is impossible to count
questions.explain_es: Propósito. Advierte de que medir el éxito distorsiona la gestión: 'The moment you measure something, you start managing for the number.'

questions.q: What is the tone of Ife's remark 'I withdraw the objection, and substitute a mild eyebrow'?
options: Weary: she wants to change topic
Hostile: she refuses his reply outright
Wry: she yields but keeps a doubt
Solemn: she apologises for a mistake
questions.explain_es: Ironía. Cede, pero con humor y dejando una pequeña reserva: 'a mild eyebrow'.

questions.q: Tobias says that councils tend to fund what they can measure.
questions.explain_es: Detalle. Lo dice así: 'Councils fund what they can measure'.

dictation: Libraries are lovely, but love isn't a funding model.
A librarian's real skill isn't knowing facts.

title: A Professional at Delay

lines.text: Ladies and gentlemen, I'd like to speak this evening about procrastination, and I promise to begin at once, just as soon as I have sharpened a few pencils.
I am, I should say, a professional. Some people dabble in delay. I have made a career of it, and I'm told the results speak for themselves, though not, as yet, to me.
Let me offer a modest proposal. Procrastination is not laziness. A lazy person does nothing, and does it with admirable calm. The procrastinator does a great deal, and all of it beside the point.
Last week, for instance, I had a report due. By Thursday I had reorganised my bookshelves by colour, descaled the kettle and written a long email to a man I haven't spoken to since school.
The report, naturally, was untouched. But I have never had a cleaner kettle, and one must find consolation where one can.

Psychologists tell me that we put things off because we want to avoid unpleasant feelings. I find this very plausible, and am delighted to have it confirmed that my failings are, in a sense, scientific.
They also tell me that the remedy is to break the task into small steps. I tried that. I broke the report into thirty small steps and have so far completed the first, which was to open the file.
Others recommend a deadline. I have found deadlines to be rather like trains. You admire them from the platform, and then they leave.

Of course there is the school of thought that says the panic of the last minute produces my best work. I hold this view with some tenderness, since it has the great advantage of being impossible to disprove.
My editor, a woman of exceptional patience, once asked whether I might hand something in early. I told her that I'd think about it, which we both understood to mean no.
Now, I would not wish to give the impression that I'm in favour of delay. I am quite firmly against it, in the abstract, as one is against bad weather.
What I would say, in all seriousness, is that a little idleness is not the enemy of thought. Many an idea has arrived while the kettle was being descaled.
The trouble begins when the idleness stops being a pause and becomes a place to live. I've visited that place. The rent is low and the view is terrible.
So if you leave here tonight with one resolution, let it be this. Do something useful tomorrow, even something small.
And if you don't, do not blame yourself too harshly. Blame me. I did tell you I was a professional.
Thank you. I would apologise for the length of this talk, but it is, I notice, the only thing I've delivered on time all year.

questions.q: What is the speaker's real attitude to his own habit of delay?
options: Proud certainty that it is harmless
Angry blame towards his editor
Deep distress about the state of his career
Wry amusement at his own failings
questions.explain_es: Actitud. Se ríe de sí mismo en lugar de sentir culpa seria: 'I am, I should say, a professional' y 'I did tell you I was a professional'.

questions.q: What does he imply by saying he told his editor 'I'd think about it'?
options: He needed time to check his schedule
He had no real intention of handing work in early
He intended to submit it the next day
His editor had misunderstood his reply
questions.explain_es: Implicatura. La frase era una negativa educada: 'which we both understood to mean no'.

questions.q: The speaker says that procrastinators do a great deal that is beside the point.
questions.explain_es: Detalle. Lo dice así: 'The procrastinator does a great deal, and all of it beside the point.'

questions.q: Why does he compare deadlines to trains?
options: To complain that trains are always late
To prove that deadlines are unreasonable
To advise listeners to travel by rail
To joke that he admires deadlines but misses them
questions.explain_es: Propósito. Es una broma sobre admirar los plazos y dejarlos pasar: 'You admire them from the platform, and then they leave.'

questions.q: What does his closing remark about delivering something on time suggest?
options: He has hardly delivered anything on time this year
His talk was the briefest he has ever given
He regards punctuality as a great virtue
He will finish his report tomorrow
questions.explain_es: Ironía. Sugiere que casi nada ha llegado a tiempo este año: 'the only thing I've delivered on time all year'.

questions.q: The speaker says that he finished last week's report before Thursday.
questions.explain_es: Detalle. Dice: 'The report, naturally, was untouched.'

dictation: The rent is low and the view is terrible.
You admire them from the platform, and then they leave.

title: Why Maps Tell Small Lies

lines.text: Good morning. Here is a question to start us off: how large is Greenland? If you've looked at a classroom wall map, you probably imagine something about the size of Africa.
In fact Africa is roughly fourteen times larger. The map, as it were, has been telling you a small lie for most of your life.
That's not a trick of memory. It's built into the way the map is drawn.

The culprit is a projection devised by the Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator, who published his famous world map in fifteen sixty-nine. It wasn't designed to mislead anyone. It was designed for sailors.
On a Mercator map a line of constant compass bearing is a straight line on the paper. For a navigator, that is worth any amount of distortion elsewhere.
The price is paid at the edges. As you move away from the equator, the map stretches shapes more and more, so lands near the poles balloon out of all proportion.
Now, no flat map can be perfectly faithful. A sphere's surface can't be flattened without something giving way. Every projection is a decision about which distortion you can live with.
So the interesting question isn't whether a map is wrong. It's whose purposes it serves, and whether we remember that it serves any.

There's a popular claim that Mercator maps were chosen to make colonial powers look bigger. I'd be wary of that. The projection suited navigation, and its later popularity owes a good deal to simple habit and to publishers' convenience.
That is not to say the effects are harmless. A generation that grows up with a map in which Europe looks large may well absorb some assumptions about who matters.
Hold on to the word 'may'. The evidence for that is thin, and I'd rather not hand you a tidy moral where there isn't one.
What I can say is that alternatives exist. Some preserve the relative sizes of countries while bending their shapes. Others compromise between the two, and look, frankly, a bit odd at first.
Odd, but honest. Many of us find a map more trustworthy when it appears to be struggling, since struggle is what flattening a sphere genuinely involves.
Which brings me to your task for next week. Choose any projection and write a paragraph explaining what it is good for. Not what it gets wrong. Everything gets something wrong.
One last remark. A map isn't a window. It is an argument, drawn very neatly, and neatness is no guarantee of truth.
Thank you. Please try to leave the room in its true proportions.

questions.q: What is the lecturer's attitude to the claim that Mercator maps were chosen to make colonial powers look bigger?
options: She finds it entirely irrelevant to geography
She regards it as a deliberate lie
She is wary of it as an oversimplification
She accepts it as clearly established fact
questions.explain_es: Actitud. Se muestra cauta: 'I'd be wary of that. The projection suited navigation'.

questions.q: What does she imply by telling students to 'hold on to the word may'?
options: Students should avoid using modal verbs
Maps certainly shape what people believe
The link between maps and attitudes is unproven
Teachers rarely agree on this evidence
questions.explain_es: Implicatura. El verbo modal marca incertidumbre: 'The evidence for that is thin, and I'd rather not hand you a tidy moral'.

questions.q: The lecturer says that a flat map cannot avoid distorting something.
questions.explain_es: Detalle. Lo dice así: 'A sphere's surface can't be flattened without something giving way.'

questions.q: Why does she mention that the Mercator projection was designed for sailors?
options: To prove that early maps were unreliable
To show that the distortion had a practical purpose
To explain why Mercator was born in Flanders
To suggest that sailors preferred inaccurate maps
questions.explain_es: Propósito. Muestra que la distorsión tenía una razón práctica, no engañosa: 'It wasn't designed to mislead anyone. It was designed for sailors.'

questions.q: How should her closing remark about leaving the room 'in its true proportions' be understood?
options: As a criticism of students' behaviour
As a joke playing on the lecture's theme
As a reminder about the next assignment
As a serious request about tidiness
questions.explain_es: Ironía. Es un juego de palabras con el tema de la distorsión de proporciones: 'Please try to leave the room in its true proportions.'

questions.q: She says that Greenland is about the same size as Africa.
questions.explain_es: Detalle. Dice: 'In fact Africa is roughly fourteen times larger.'

dictation: Every projection is a decision about which distortion you can live with.

title: Who Decides What Counts as a Word?

lines.text: Welcome to Word of Mouth. Today's guest compiles dictionaries, which I'd always assumed was a job for people who have never been invited to parties. Joan Pryce, am I being unfair?
Entirely fair. We do tend to be found near the quiet end of the room, usually checking how somebody has used a semicolon.
Let's begin with the big question. Who decides what's a word?

Nobody decides, which disappoints people. A dictionary doesn't confer words, it records them. We watch how people actually write and speak, and when a word has been used by enough people over enough time, we add it.
How much is enough?

There's no magic number. We look for a word turning up in different sources, over a span of years, with a consistent meaning. A word used once in a famous message is a curiosity. A word used everywhere for five years is a candidate.
I imagine you get angry letters.

Constantly. Usually about words people feel are ruining the language. The charge is almost always that a word is 'not real', and it's very hard to explain that a word you can hear is, by definition, real.
Some complain that you shouldn't include slang at all.

And some complain that we left it out. We can't win, and we've made our peace with that. I'd add that today's slang is quite often tomorrow's standard vocabulary, and many a word now considered perfectly respectable was once frowned upon.
Do you have a favourite word?

I'm suspicious of people who do, but I'll play along. I'm fond of 'petrichor', the smell of rain on dry ground. Two Australian scientists coined it in the nineteen sixties, and I like that the experience was there for centuries before anyone gave it a name.
That's rather lovely. Is there a word you'd keep out if you could?
In my professional capacity, no. In my private capacity, there are several, and I'll take them to my grave.
A fine distinction.
I find it keeps me employed and sane, usually in that order.
Joan, final question. Is English getting worse?
Every generation says so, and every generation has been wrong. Complaints that the language is in decline are, if anything, among its oldest traditions.
Joan Pryce, thank you.
Thank you. And do check your semicolons.

questions.q: What is Joan's attitude to complaints about the words her dictionary includes or omits?
options: Delighted pride at being criticised
Indifference to whether words are real
Furious resentment towards correspondents
Patient resignation about unavoidable complaints
questions.explain_es: Actitud. Se resigna con calma: 'We can't win, and we've made our peace with that.'

questions.q: What does Joan imply by saying 'In my private capacity, there are several' words she would keep out?
options: She never forms opinions about words
She includes only words she personally likes
She keeps her private tastes out of her work
She secretly excludes words she dislikes
questions.explain_es: Implicatura. Separa sus gustos privados de su trabajo profesional: 'In my professional capacity, no.'

questions.q: Joan says that a word must appear in varied sources over several years before it is added.
questions.explain_es: Detalle. Dice: 'We look for a word turning up in different sources, over a span of years'.

questions.q: Why does Joan mention the word 'petrichor'?
options: To show that things can exist before they are named
To prove that scientists invent most new words
To recommend it as a word for beginners
To argue that old words are always better
questions.explain_es: Propósito. Ilustra que la experiencia existía antes de la palabra: 'the experience was there for centuries before anyone gave it a name'.

questions.q: How does Joan respond to the host's joke about people never invited to parties?
options: She plays along with self-mocking humour
She corrects him with solemn precision
She pretends not to have heard it
She takes offence at the stereotype
questions.explain_es: Ironía. Sigue la broma riéndose de sí misma: 'We do tend to be found near the quiet end of the room'.

questions.q: Joan says that a dictionary decides which words are officially real.
questions.explain_es: Detalle. Dice: 'A dictionary doesn't confer words, it records them.'

dictation: A dictionary doesn't confer words, it records them.
Complaints that the language is in decline are, if anything, among its oldest traditions.

title: Does Nostalgia Do More Harm Than Good?
focus: Concession, qualification and humour in debate

lines.text: Good evening. The motion is: nostalgia does more harm than good. Professor Rahim speaks for the motion, Doctor Carter against. Professor, you have five minutes, though I notice you've brought a rather long set of notes.

I have, and I'd ask the audience to remember that I'm not against memory. I'm against the particular habit of mistaking memory for a verdict. Nostalgia tells us the past was warmer, simpler and better, and it does so on remarkably little evidence.
It is also useful to those in power. A politician who promises to restore a golden age needn't specify which year, which rules or which people were doing the suffering.
That's a splendid speech about nostalgia as a political tool. I'm afraid it isn't a speech about nostalgia as a human experience, which is what most of us actually have.

Researchers have found that people who reflect on warm memories tend to report feeling more connected, more optimistic, even a touch less lonely. These are modest effects, and I wouldn't oversell them, but they aren't nothing.
I'm happy to grant a short-term lift in mood. So does a sugary snack. The question is what we do with the feeling.
Which is a fair point, though I'd say it applies to any emotion. Anger can be corrosive too, and nobody has proposed abolishing it.
Somebody should.
Order, order. Professor, was that a serious proposal?
It was a joke, Chair, at the expense of my own argument. I concede the point.
Then I'll be generous in return. Where nostalgia becomes unhealthy is when it replaces the present, when someone ends up living in an album.
On that we can agree. A photograph is a lovely place to visit, and a poor place to move to.
And yet most people use nostalgia as a visit, not a move. That, I'd suggest, is why it endures.
Professor, you've accepted that, so does the motion fall?
I'd say it wobbles. The evidence of harm is mostly about misuse, not the feeling itself, and I'm honest enough to admit that.
I'll take a wobble. I came prepared for a fight and I'm, frankly, quite happy to leave with a draw.
Then the audience will decide. Please vote as you leave, preferably without sentimentality.

questions.q: What is Professor Rahim's attitude to nostalgia?
options: She enjoys it but fears its popularity
She dismisses all positive emotions
She distrusts it as a verdict on the past
She believes it harms everyone's memory
questions.explain_es: Actitud. No ataca el recuerdo sino su uso como juicio: 'I'm against the particular habit of mistaking memory for a verdict.'

questions.q: What does Professor Rahim imply about a politician who promises to restore a golden age?
options: Golden ages are easy to define precisely
Voters always know which year is meant
Such promises depend on vagueness about the past
Politicians deliberately choose the wrong year
questions.explain_es: Implicatura. La promesa funciona precisamente por su vaguedad: 'needn't specify which year, which rules or which people were doing the suffering'.

questions.q: Doctor Carter says that the positive effects found by researchers are modest.
questions.explain_es: Detalle. Dice: 'These are modest effects, and I wouldn't oversell them'.

questions.q: Why does Doctor Carter say that anger 'can be corrosive too'?
options: To agree that emotions should be banned
To argue that the risks are not unique to nostalgia
To show that anger is more common than nostalgia
To claim that nostalgia and anger are identical
questions.explain_es: Propósito. Responde que el riesgo de abuso se aplica a cualquier emoción: 'it applies to any emotion'.

questions.q: How should the Professor's interjection 'Somebody should' be understood?
options: As a joke about the idea of abolishing anger
As a serious call to ban anger
As an angry interruption of Doctor Carter
As a rebuke to the chair
questions.explain_es: Ironía. Ella misma lo aclara: 'It was a joke, Chair, at the expense of my own argument.'
